PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

This sub-strand builds careful listening and clear speech around food and health. You will hear the sounds /ʊ/, /uː/, /æ/, /f/ and /v/, answer questions about a short passage, use words such as nutrition, vitamin, protein and deficiency, and say sentences with the pattern 'noun phrase + would like to be'.

## Strand 5.0: Nutrition - Balanced Diet
Sub-strand 5.1.1: Listening and Speaking: Pronunciation and Vocabulary
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) listen actively to a variety of texts to gain information
b) apply vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts for effective communication
c) use the language pattern correctly for effective oral communication
d) promote listening to a variety of texts for information and enjoyment

## What this sub-strand covers
• Listening Comprehension
• Language Pattern (noun phrase + would like to be ...)

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we listen carefully?
2. How can we improve our pronunciation?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is enhanced as the learner participates in sharing their thoughts as they discuss collaboratively.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: This is cultivated as the learner is able to draw conclusions from the listening text.

## Values
• Love: This is cultivated as the learner is able to portray a caring attitude to special groups of people that require meals with diverse nutritional value.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Prevention of lifestyle or non-communicable diseases: This is promoted as the learner is informed on a balanced diet for varied nutritional needs.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the theme of nutrition to their learning in Agriculture.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 5.0 Nutrition – Balanced Diet, Sub-strand 5.1.1 Pronunciation and Vocabulary

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Listening for sounds and for meaning

LESSON 1: LISTENING FOR SOUNDS AND FOR MEANING
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Hear and say /ʊ/, /uː/, /æ/, /f/ and /v/ in words about food.
• Answer questions about a passage that is read aloud.
• Explain how careful listening helps you keep the facts straight.

Curriculum outcomes: a) listen actively to a variety of texts to gain information; d) promote listening to a variety of texts for information and enjoyment

## Introduction
A cook can say 'fruit' and a listener can hear 'foot'. Those words are not the same food advice. Listening for single sounds, and listening for the meaning of a whole passage, are two skills you need at the same time.

## Notes
### Five sounds to hear
The marks between slashes show sounds.

- /ʊ/ is short. You hear it in look, good, cook, put and foot.
- /uː/ is longer. You hear it in food, fruit, juice, soup, school and too.
- /æ/ is the short a in habit, fat, apple, salad, family, packed and mango.
- /f/ is a quiet stream of air. Your top teeth touch your lower lip, and your throat does not buzz. You hear it in food, fruit, fish, safe and family.
- /v/ uses the same teeth and lip, but your throat buzzes. You hear it in vitamin, vegetable, very and have.

Put your fingers on your throat. Say /f/ and you feel little. Say /v/ and you feel a buzz. Fat and vat are a minimal pair: only that buzz changes the word.

### A passage to listen to
Ask someone to read this aloud once while you listen, without reading. Then they may read it again.

The school cook put a jug of water on the table and looked at the class. 'Good food is a habit,' she said. 'Ugali and other carbohydrates give us energy. Beans and fish give us protein to build the body. Fruit, such as a mango or an apple, gives us vitamins. Vegetables give us vitamins too. A meal that leaves out a whole group is not balanced.'

Zawadi put up her hand. 'My family would like to be healthy,' she said. 'We have packed fruit instead of too many sweets.'

The cook nodded. 'Too much sugar and too much fat, with very little play, can harm the body over time. If a child is very weak, or has swollen feet, tell an adult. A health worker should check that child. Do not invent a name for the illness yourself.'

### Questions a careful listener can answer
Who spoke first? What did she put on the table? Which foods did she link to energy, to protein and to vitamins? What should you do if a child is very weak or has swollen feet?

You cannot answer well if you were talking during the reading. Look at the speaker, keep your hands still, and hold your question until the end. Then answer from the passage, not from a guess.

## Key words
• nutrition — the way food helps the body grow, get energy and stay well
• vitamin — a substance the body needs in small amounts, found in foods such as fruit and vegetables
• carbohydrates — energy foods such as ugali, rice, bread and potatoes
• minimal pair — two words that differ by only one sound, such as fat and vat

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which word has /uː/: foot, food or cook?

Working:
1. Say the three words.
2. Foot and cook have the short /ʊ/. Food has the long /uː/.

Answer: food

### Example 2
From the passage, which foods give protein?

Working:
1. Recall the cook's sentence about building the body.
2. She named beans and fish.

Answer: Beans and fish

## Activity: Listen, then answer
You will need: The passage read by the teacher or played from a recording, Slates or exercise books
1. Listen to the passage once with books closed.
2. In pairs, say the words look, food, habit, fruit and vitamin, and name the target sound in each.
3. Answer four questions the teacher asks. Use words from the passage.
4. Discuss why you listened a second time: which fact became clearer?

## Practice
1. How can you feel the difference between /f/ and /v/?
2. According to the cook, what should you do if a child is very weak or has swollen feet?
3. Write two words with /æ/ from the lesson.

## Summary
• /ʊ/ as in cook, /uː/ as in food, /æ/ as in habit, /f/ as in fruit, /v/ as in vitamin.
• Listen to the whole passage before you answer.
• Answer from what the speaker said.

### Answers to practice
1. Put your fingers on your throat. /v/ buzzes and /f/ does not. Both use the top teeth on the lower lip.
2. Tell an adult so a health worker can check the child. Do not invent the name of the illness.
3. Any two of: habit, fat, apple, salad, family, packed, mango.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Words for a balanced diet

LESSON 2: WORDS FOR A BALANCED DIET
===================================

## What you will learn
• Explain nutrition words in simple, accurate sentences.
• Group foods as energy foods, body-building foods and protective foods.
• Talk about deficiency, anaemia, kwashiorkor, marasmus and obesity without teasing anyone.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts for effective communication

## Introduction
Calling every meal 'healthy' does not help anyone plan a plate. The words protein, vitamin, fat and deficiency let you say exactly what the body is getting, and what it may be missing.

## Notes
### Food and what it does
Nutrition is the way food serves the body. A diet is the food and drink a person usually has. A balanced diet includes energy foods, body-building foods and protective foods, plus clean water, in amounts that suit the person.

- Carbohydrates give energy. Ugali, rice, bread, potatoes and cassava belong here.
- Proteins build and repair the body. Beans, peas, eggs, milk, fish, meat and groundnuts are useful sources.
- Vitamins and minerals protect the body and help it work. Fruit and vegetables, such as mangoes, oranges, carrots and sukuma wiki, supply many of them.
- Fats and oils also give energy and help the body use some vitamins. Avocado and a little cooking oil fit here. A plate that is mostly fat is not balanced.
- Water is not a vitamin, but the body needs it every day.

Sugar can make food sweet, but sweets and sugary drinks do not replace fruit. Too much sugar helps cause tooth decay.

### When the diet is not enough
A deficiency means the body is not getting enough of something it needs.

In class we learn that kwashiorkor is linked with a diet that does not provide enough protein. A child may have swollen feet, legs or face, a swollen belly, thin arms, and hair that becomes thin or changes colour. The child may be miserable and not grow well. Marasmus is linked with too little energy food and too little protein. The child becomes very thin and may look older than they are. Both are serious. Only a health worker should decide what is wrong, and the treatment is proper food and medical care, not a guess by friends.

Anaemia means the blood is not carrying enough oxygen. One common reason is too little iron. The person may feel tired, weak or dizzy, and may look pale. Tiredness has other causes too, including illness, so an adult should ask a health worker. Iron is found in meat, beans, eggs and dark green leafy vegetables.

Obesity means having so much extra body fat that health can suffer. It can develop when someone often takes in more energy than the body uses. It is not a joke and not a reason to mock anyone. People have different bodies. We can still learn that plenty of vegetables, fruit, water and daily play, and fewer sugary drinks, help the body.

Plump and thin are describing words. They do not, by themselves, tell you that someone is ill. A child who is becoming very weak, very thin, or swollen needs an adult, not a nickname.

## Key words
• balanced diet — a way of eating that gives the body energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods and water in suitable amounts
• protein — the part of food that helps the body grow and repair itself
• deficiency — a lack of something the body needs
• anaemia — a condition in which the blood does not carry enough oxygen; too little iron is one common cause
• habit — something a person does so often that it becomes usual

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which group does sukuma wiki belong to, and why?

Working:
1. Sukuma wiki is a dark green vegetable.
2. Vegetables are protective foods because they supply vitamins and minerals.

Answer: Protective foods. It supplies vitamins and minerals.

### Example 2
A classmate calls a thin child 'marasmus' as a joke. What is wrong with that?

Working:
1. Marasmus is a serious condition, not an insult.
2. Being thin does not prove an illness, and only a health worker should make that judgement.

Answer: It is unkind and untrue as a label. Tell an adult if a child seems very weak or ill. Do not diagnose or tease.

## Activity: Sort the plate
You will need: Word cards: ugali, beans, mango, cooking oil, water, sweets, fish, sukuma wiki, milk, Three labelled sheets: Energy, Body-building, Protective
1. In groups, place each food card on the sheet where it belongs. Water and sweets need a sentence, not only a pile.
2. Explain one card using the words protein, vitamin, carbohydrate or fat.
3. Discuss, kindly, why plump and thin should not be used as insults.
4. Say what an adult should do if a child has swollen feet or is too weak to play.

## Practice
1. Name one carbohydrate food and one protein food.
2. What is a deficiency?
3. Why should children not decide that a classmate has kwashiorkor?
4. What is one problem caused by too much sugar?

## Summary
• A balanced diet has energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods and water.
• Kwashiorkor, marasmus and anaemia are health problems for a health worker to identify.
• Use body words kindly. Report real weakness or swelling to an adult.

### Answers to practice
1. Carbohydrate: ugali, rice, bread, potatoes or cassava. Protein: beans, eggs, milk, fish, meat or groundnuts.
2. A lack of something the body needs.
3. Only a health worker can tell what is wrong. Swollen feet or weakness should be reported to an adult, not turned into a nickname.
4. Tooth decay. Sugary foods also do not replace the vitamins in fruit.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: The pattern 'would like to be'

LESSON 3: THE PATTERN 'WOULD LIKE TO BE'
========================================

## What you will learn
• Say sentences in the pattern noun phrase + would like to be.
• Retell a short food story in the right order.
• State the lesson the story teaches.

Curriculum outcomes: c) use the language pattern correctly for effective oral communication; d) promote listening to a variety of texts for information and enjoyment

## Introduction
Zawadi would like to be strong. The cook would like to be helpful. This pattern tells us a wish about the future. It is more than a list of foods. It says who wants to become what.

## Notes
### How the pattern is built
A noun phrase names who or what we are talking about. Then we add would like to be, and then a noun or an adjective.

- Zawadi would like to be a cook.
- The pupils would like to be healthy.
- My family would like to be careful about sugar.
- The school club would like to be a place where we share fruit.

Would like to be is a polite way to talk about a wish. It is not the same as would like plus a thing. I would like an apple means you want an apple now. I would like to be strong means you want that state for yourself.

In speech, would often joins the pronoun: I'd like to be healthy. In class, say the full words first so the pattern stays clear. The negative is would not like to be: I would not like to be careless with my meals.

### A story to retell
Listen, then tell it again in your own words.

On Monday the cook told a story about two brothers. The older brother ate only ugali and sweet tea. He refused fruit and beans. By afternoon he felt tired, and his teacher sent him to drink water and to rest. The younger brother packed a banana, some groundnuts and a boiled egg. He would like to be a footballer, so he ate food that could help him play.

Their mother listened that evening. 'I would like to be fair to both of you,' she said. She put sukuma wiki and beans on the table beside the ugali, and she kept the sugar jar for a small spoon in the tea, not for a second cup of sweets.

The older brother said, 'I would like to be well enough for games.' He tasted the beans.

The lesson is not that ugali is bad. Ugali gives energy. The lesson is that one food, or a lot of sugar, does not make a balanced diet. People who are ill, very young, or expecting a baby need meals that suit them, and a health worker or a parent should guide those meals.

### Retelling well
Keep the order: the cook's story, the two lunches, the mother's decision, the brother's wish. Use the names. Do not add a miracle cure. Changing one supper does not remove a serious illness, but a better habit can begin at the next meal.

## Key words
• noun phrase — a word or group of words that names a person, place or thing, such as my family or the school cook
• would like to be — a polite pattern used to say what someone wishes to become or to be like
• retell — to tell a story again in your own words, keeping the important facts in order

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Make a sentence with the noun phrase 'the children' and the wish 'healthy'.

Working:
1. Start with the noun phrase.
2. Add would like to be, then the adjective.

Answer: The children would like to be healthy.

### Example 2
What lesson did the mother's meal teach?

Working:
1. She kept the ugali and added beans and sukuma wiki.
2. She limited the sugar.

Answer: A meal needs more than one kind of food. Ugali can stay, with protein and vegetables, and sugar should be limited.

## Activity: Dramatise and discuss the lesson
You will need: The story of the two brothers, Simple props such as a jug, a book for a sugar jar, and fruit if the class has some
1. In groups of four, take the parts of the cook, the two brothers and the mother.
2. Act the story. Each brother must say one sentence with would like to be.
3. Retell the story as a group in five or six spoken sentences, in order.
4. Discuss the lesson you learnt, including how to talk about a tired classmate without naming a disease you are not sure of.

## Practice
1. Complete the pattern: My uncle ____ a nurse.
2. What is the difference between 'I would like a mango' and 'I would like to be strong'?
3. In the story, why was ugali not called a bad food?
4. Write one lesson from the story in your own words.

## Summary
• Noun phrase + would like to be + noun or adjective states a wish.
• Retell events in order and keep the facts.
• A better meal can start a healthy habit. It is not a child's job to diagnose illness.

### Answers to practice
1. My uncle would like to be a nurse.
2. The first asks for a thing now. The second states a wish about yourself.
3. Ugali is a carbohydrate and gives energy. The problem was eating it without other food groups and taking a lot of sugar.
4. A balanced meal includes more than one food group, and a serious illness should be left to a health worker and a parent.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 5.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word has the long sound /uː/?
   A. cook
   B. foot
   C. fruit
   D. put

2. Which pair is a minimal pair for /f/ and /v/?
   A. food and fruit
   B. fat and vat
   C. look and cook
   D. bean and meat

3. In the cook's passage, beans and fish were linked to
   A. protein
   B. only sugar
   C. luggage
   D. a number plate

4. A balanced diet includes
   A. only sweets
   B. energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods and water
   C. fat and nothing else
   D. water only

5. Which statement about kwashiorkor is the safe one?
   A. Classmates should label a thin child with the word
   B. It is linked with too little protein and a health worker should be involved if a child is swollen or very weak
   C. It is cured by one sweet
   D. It means the same thing as a broken bone

6. Anaemia that comes from too little iron may make a person
   A. grow extra hair overnight
   B. feel tired and weak
   C. need a number plate
   D. stop drinking water forever

7. Choose the correct pattern.
   A. Would like to be the pupils healthy.
   B. The pupils would like to be healthy.
   C. Healthy would like pupils be.
   D. The pupils like would healthy be.

8. 'I would like an orange' means
   A. I want to become an orange
   B. I want an orange
   C. I refuse fruit
   D. I am a cook

9. Why do we listen to a passage before we answer?
   A. So we can invent extra facts
   B. So our answers come from what was said
   C. So we can skip the vitamins
   D. So we never retell stories

10. Write a sentence using 'my sister' and 'would like to be' about health.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 5.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

1. C. fruit
   Fruit has /uː/. Cook, foot and put have the short /ʊ/.

2. B. fat and vat
   Fat and vat differ by the buzz of the voice.

3. A. protein
   She said beans and fish give protein to build the body.

4. B. energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods and water
   The body needs the different food groups and water.

5. B. It is linked with too little protein and a health worker should be involved if a child is swollen or very weak
   The diet link is a lack of enough protein, and diagnosis belongs to a health worker.

6. B. feel tired and weak
   Tiredness and paleness can be signs. A health worker should check, because tiredness has many causes.

7. B. The pupils would like to be healthy.
   The noun phrase comes first, then would like to be, then the adjective.

8. B. I want an orange
   Would like plus a noun asks for a thing. Would like to be states what you wish to be.

9. B. So our answers come from what was said
   Careful listening keeps the information accurate.

10. My sister would like to be healthy.
   The noun phrase my sister is followed by would like to be and an adjective.

Working:
1. Marasmus is a serious condition, not an insult.
2. Being thin does not prove an illness, and only a health worker should make that judgement.

Answer: It is unkind and untrue as a label. Tell an adult if a child seems very weak or ill. Do not diagnose or tease.

## Activity: Sort the plate
You will need: Word cards: ugali, beans, mango, cooking oil, water, sweets, fish, sukuma wiki, milk, Three labelled sheets: Energy, Body-building, Protective
1. In groups, place each food card on the sheet where it belongs. Water and sweets need a sentence, not only a pile.
2. Explain one card using the words protein, vitamin, carbohydrate or fat.
3. Discuss, kindly, why plump and thin should not be used as insults.
4. Say what an adult should do if a child has swollen feet or is too weak to play.

## Practice
1. Name one carbohydrate food and one protein food.
2. What is a deficiency?
3. Why should children not decide that a classmate has kwashiorkor?
4. What is one problem caused by too much sugar?

## Summary
• A balanced diet has energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods and water.
• Kwashiorkor, marasmus and anaemia are health problems for a health worker to identify.
• Use body words kindly. Report real weakness or swelling to an adult.

### Answers to practice
1. Carbohydrate: ugali, rice, bread, potatoes or cassava. Protein: beans, eggs, milk, fish, meat or groundnuts.
2. A lack of something the body needs.
3. Only a health worker can tell what is wrong. Swollen feet or weakness should be reported to an adult, not turned into a nickname.
4. Tooth decay. Sugary foods also do not replace the vitamins in fruit.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: The pattern 'would like to be'
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: THE PATTERN 'WOULD LIKE TO BE'
========================================

## What you will learn
• Say sentences in the pattern noun phrase + would like to be.
• Retell a short food story in the right order.
• State the lesson the story teaches.

Curriculum outcomes: c) use the language pattern correctly for effective oral communication; d) promote listening to a variety of texts for information and enjoyment

## Introduction
Zawadi would like to be strong. The cook would like to be helpful. This pattern tells us a wish about the future. It is more than a list of foods. It says who wants to become what.

## Notes
### How the pattern is built
A noun phrase names who or what we are talking about. Then we add would like to be, and then a noun or an adjective.

- Zawadi would like to be a cook.
- The pupils would like to be healthy.
- My family would like to be careful about sugar.
- The school club would like to be a place where we share fruit.

Would like to be is a polite way to talk about a wish. It is not the same as would like plus a thing. I would like an apple means you want an apple now. I would like to be strong means you want that state for yourself.

In speech, would often joins the pronoun: I'd like to be healthy. In class, say the full words first so the pattern stays clear. The negative is would not like to be: I would not like to be careless with my meals.

### A story to retell
Listen, then tell it again in your own words.

On Monday the cook told a story about two brothers. The older brother ate only ugali and sweet tea. He refused fruit and beans. By afternoon he felt tired, and his teacher sent him to drink water and to rest. The younger brother packed a banana, some groundnuts and a boiled egg. He would like to be a footballer, so he ate food that could help him play.

Their mother listened that evening. 'I would like to be fair to both of you,' she said. She put sukuma wiki and beans on the table beside the ugali, and she kept the sugar jar for a small spoon in the tea, not for a second cup of sweets.

The older brother said, 'I would like to be well enough for games.' He tasted the beans.

The lesson is not that ugali is bad. Ugali gives energy. The lesson is that one food, or a lot of sugar, does not make a balanced diet. People who are ill, very young, or expecting a baby need meals that suit them, and a health worker or a parent should guide those meals.

### Retelling well
Keep the order: the cook's story, the two lunches, the mother's decision, the brother's wish. Use the names. Do not add a miracle cure. Changing one supper does not remove a serious illness, but a better habit can begin at the next meal.

## Key words
• noun phrase — a word or group of words that names a person, place or thing, such as my family or the school cook
• would like to be — a polite pattern used to say what someone wishes to become or to be like
• retell — to tell a story again in your own words, keeping the important facts in order

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Make a sentence with the noun phrase 'the children' and the wish 'healthy'.

Working:
1. Start with the noun phrase.
2. Add would like to be, then the adjective.

Answer: The children would like to be healthy.

### Example 2
What lesson did the mother's meal teach?

Working:
1. She kept the ugali and added beans and sukuma wiki.
2. She limited the sugar.

Answer: A meal needs more than one kind of food. Ugali can stay, with protein and vegetables, and sugar should be limited.

## Activity: Dramatise and discuss the lesson
You will need: The story of the two brothers, Simple props such as a jug, a book for a sugar jar, and fruit if the class has some
1. In groups of four, take the parts of the cook, the two brothers and the mother.
2. Act the story. Each brother must say one sentence with would like to be.
3. Retell the story as a group in five or six spoken sentences, in order.
4. Discuss the lesson you learnt, including how to talk about a tired classmate without naming a disease you are not sure of.

## Practice
1. Complete the pattern: My uncle ____ a nurse.
2. What is the difference between 'I would like a mango' and 'I would like to be strong'?
3. In the story, why was ugali not called a bad food?
4. Write one lesson from the story in your own words.

## Summary
• Noun phrase + would like to be + noun or adjective states a wish.
• Retell events in order and keep the facts.
• A better meal can start a healthy habit. It is not a child's job to diagnose illness.

### Answers to practice
1. My uncle would like to be a nurse.
2. The first asks for a thing now. The second states a wish about yourself.
3. Ugali is a carbohydrate and gives energy. The problem was eating it without other food groups and taking a lot of sugar.
4. A balanced meal includes more than one food group, and a serious illness should be left to a health worker and a parent.

questions.question: Which word has the long sound /uː/?
questions.explanation: Fruit has /uː/. Cook, foot and put have the short /ʊ/.

questions.question: Which pair is a minimal pair for /f/ and /v/?
questions.explanation: Fat and vat differ by the buzz of the voice.

questions.question: In the cook's passage, beans and fish were linked to
questions.explanation: She said beans and fish give protein to build the body.

questions.question: A balanced diet includes
options: energy foods, body-building foods, protective foods and water
questions.explanation: The body needs the different food groups and water.

questions.question: Which statement about kwashiorkor is the safe one?
options: Classmates should label a thin child with the word
It is linked with too little protein and a health worker should be involved if a child is swollen or very weak
It is cured by one sweet
It means the same thing as a broken bone
questions.explanation: The diet link is a lack of enough protein, and diagnosis belongs to a health worker.

questions.question: Anaemia that comes from too little iron may make a person
questions.explanation: Tiredness and paleness can be signs. A health worker should check, because tiredness has many causes.

questions.question: Choose the correct pattern.
options: Would like to be the pupils healthy.
The pupils would like to be healthy.
The pupils like would healthy be.
questions.explanation: The noun phrase comes first, then would like to be, then the adjective.

questions.question: 'I would like an orange' means
options: I want to become an orange
questions.explanation: Would like plus a noun asks for a thing. Would like to be states what you wish to be.

questions.question: Why do we listen to a passage before we answer?
options: So we can invent extra facts
So our answers come from what was said
So we can skip the vitamins
questions.explanation: Careful listening keeps the information accurate.

questions.question: Write a sentence using 'my sister' and 'would like to be' about health.
questions.answer: My sister would like to be healthy.
questions.explanation: The noun phrase my sister is followed by would like to be and an adjective.
